Methods: Individuals visiting 182 primary care physicians (PCPs) across
5 countries over a 2-week period completed a ’diagnostic questionnaire ’
consistent with the International RLS Study Group diagnostic criteria.
Patients whose symptoms met the criteria and experienced symptoms at
least one day a week completed a further questionnaire on their symptoms.
The PCP also completed a questionnaire on the medical history and current
treatment of these patients.
Results: 23,052 individuals completed the diagnostic questionnaire and
2223 (9.6%) satis ﬁed the criteria for RLS occurring at least once a week
(RLSQ/H11001patients). Twenty-three percent of the RLSQ /H11001patients reported
symptoms occurring daily and 35% reported they occurred at least 4 days
per week. A matching pair of patient and PCP questionnaires were received
for 1557 (70.0%) of these individuals. Before ﬁlling in their questionnaire,
PCPs were asked what diagnosis had been given for symptoms that
satisﬁed the diagnostic criteria. The proportion of patients who were
RLSQ/H11001varied across the 5 countries. The percentage of RLSQ /H11001patients
who were diagnosed by the PCP also varied across the 5 countries.
Conclusions: The proportion of the population that visits a PCP and has
symptoms consistent with the RLS diagnostic criteria varied (4.5 –19.1%)
across the countries researched. Patients suffering from frequent symptoms
of RLS suffer marked sleep disturbance and decreased quality of life (1).
This research reveals that a signi ﬁcant number of these patients, many with
daily symptoms, despite visiting and discussing their symptoms with their
PCP are not given a diagnosis of RLS nor appear to be getting treatment
speciﬁc for RLS.
1. Allen RP, Earley CJ. J Clin Neurophysiol 2001;18:128 –147.
P775
Restless legs syndrome in Parkinson ’s disease: A case-control study
M. Behari, P. R. Krishnan, M. Bhatia (New Delhi, India)
Background: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common sleep disorder
that occurs frequently in patients with Parkinson ’s disease (PD).
Objective: To estimate the prevalence of RLS in Indian PD patients.
Methods: One hundred twenty six consecutive PD patients were re-
cruited along with 128 healthy age and sex matched controls. The patients
with PD were assessed in a face-to-face interview using a predesigned
questionnaire.
Results: RLS was seen in 10 of 126 cases of PD (7.6%) and one of 128
controls (1.28%, P /H110050.013). PD patients with RLS were older than those
without RLS (63.70 /H110067.80 years vs.57.37 /H1100610.04 years, P /H110050.05), and
had higher prevalence of depression (40% vs.10.3%, P /H110050.023). In
addition, PD patient with depression and RLS had a higher Epworth
Sleepiness Scale Score (ESS) (11.25 /H110067.14 vs.3.33 /H110061.97, P /H110050.030)
and were receiving higher dose of levodopa (987.5 /H11005/-560.32 vs.370 /H11006
185.74 mg/day, P /H110050.05). No demographic factors or factors related to PD
i.e., side of involvement, age of onset, duration of PD, Hoehn and Yahr
stage or UPDRS subset scores correlated with the presence or severity of
RLS.
Conclusions: RLS is more common among patients with PD than con-
trols. A greater medical recognition of this disorder is needed in view of
available effective treatment.
P776
Rotigotine CDS (Constant Delivery System) in the treatment of mod-
erate to advanced stages of Restless Legs Syndrome: A double-blind,
placebo-controlled pilot study

K. Stiasny, H. Benes, R. Bodenschatz, J. C. Moller, E. Schollmayer,
W. H. Oertel, RTG Study Group (Marburg, Germany; Schwarz Pharma)
Objective/Background: Dopaminergic drugs such as levodopa or dopa-
mine agonists are currently considered the ﬁrst-line treatment for restless-
legs-syndrome (RLS). However, long-term treatment with levodopa may
cause deterioration of symptoms (i.e., augmentation or time-shifting) in a
substantial part of RLS patients. Dopamine agonists (DA) in particuliar
long-acting substances are preferred in moderate to severe RLS but even
under DAs augmentation occurs. Different trials suggest an inverse corre-
lation between elimination half-life and incidence of augmentation. We
therefore investigated the ef ﬁcacy and safety of a novel transdermal patch
continuously releasing the dopamine agonist rotigotine (RTG) in moderate
to advanced stages of RLS.
Methods: We performed a double-blind, 4-arm, parallel group, random-
ised, placebo-controlled pilot study in 9 German centers. Main inclusion
criterion was the diagnosis of idiopathic moderate to advanced RLS de-
ﬁned by a score of /H1135010 in the IRLSSG severity scale (maximum 40 pts),
when untreated, and the presence of day-time symptoms. After a wash-out
phase of 7 /H110064 days, patients received 1.125 mg RTG/day, 2.25 mg
RTG/day, 4.5 mg RTG/day, or placebo for 7 /H110061 days. Primary endpoint
was the change of the IRLSSG severity scale from baseline to the end of
treatment.
Results: 63 of 68 enrolled patients were randomized and used for
statistical evaluation. A dose-dependent reduction in RLS severity was
observed in all treatment arms resulting in a net bene ﬁt of 1.3 (1.125 mg
RTG/day; P /H110050.38), 3.6 (2.25 mg RTG/day; P /H110050.09), and 6.3 points on
the IRLSSG severity scale (4.5 mg RTG/day; P /H110050.04) as compared to the
placebo arm. Obvious differences regarding the topical tolerability of the
patch or its systemic side effects were not found between the verum and
placebo patches.
Conclusions: This study suggests a clear clinical ef ﬁcacy of rotigotine
for the treatment of moderate to advanced RLS. Since this investigation
was designed as a pilot study, its results are not yet suf ﬁciently powered
and will accordingly be con ﬁrmed by subsequent studies.
P777
Stiff-person syndrome associated with anti-amphiphysin antibodies:
Neuropathology and antibody-binding studies
M. Naumann, C. Sommer, C. Wessig, K. Toyka (Wu ¨rzburg, Germany)
Background: Stiff-person syndrome is a rare neurological disorder char-
acterized by progressive rigidity and superimposed spasms. In some cases,
it occurs as a paraneoplastic syndrome in patients with breast carcinoma or
small-cell lung carcinoma. The disease is considered to be autoimmune-
mediated as it is associated with antibodies to the GABA-synthesizing
enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) in more than 60 % or, in some
cases, with antibodies to amphiphysin, a 128-kD synaptic protein.
Case Report: We report on a 71 years old female patient who developed
an anti-amphiphysin associated stiff-person syndrome and encephalopathy
before the diagnosis of a breast carcinoma was made. Initially, the patient ’s
symptoms responded well to plasmapheresis with subsequent decline of
serum anti-amphiphysin antibodies and immunosuppressive therapy. The
patient ﬁnally died from progressive encephalopathy and stiffness which
were resistant to any treatment.
We demonstrate for the ﬁrst time neuropathological and imunhisto-

chemical ﬁndings in brain and spinal cord tissue of an anti-amphysin
antibody associated stiff-person syndrome. These changes are correlated to
experimental ﬁndings with anti-amphiphysin antibodies in rat tissue. Bind-
ing studies with the patient ’s serum revealed strong binding to human and
spinal cord axons and to neurons and microglial cells in human brain.
Furthermore, binding of endogenous IgG on autopsy sections of the pa-
tient’s brain could be demonstrated.
Conclusion: In stiff-person syndrome, anti-amphiphysin antibodies bind
to synaptic structures at various levels of the human and rat CNS, partic-
ularly the spinal cord. As the disease progresses in ﬂammatory in ﬁltrates
predominate leading to progressive neuronal damage.
P778
Stiff-person syndrome presenting with asymmetric axial muscle
spasms and hypertrophy
C. Chuang (New York, NY, USA)
Objective: To describe an atypical presentation of Stiff-person
syndrome.
Background: Stiff-Person syndrome is a condition of continuous motor
unit activity which results in symmetric axial and proximal muscle rigidity
with superimposed episodic muscle spasms. The symptoms are usually
responsive to benzodiazepines and other GABAergic drugs. An asymmet-

ric subtype, involving a single limb, has been labelled as Stiff-Limb
Syndrome. However, asymmetric involvement of axial musculature has
never been described in the literature.
Methods: A Medline literature search of Stiff-person syndrome was
performed to review all previously described cases. A detailed history was
obtained from our patient and clinical examination was documented by
videotape. The diagnosis of Stiff-Person syndrome was con ﬁrmed by
electromyographic evidence of continuous motor unit activity and clinical
evidence of improvement with intravenous diazepam during an episodic
muscle spasm.
Results: The patient is a 37 year-old, right-handed woman with a history
of cervical radiculopathy and carpal tunnel syndrome who presented to the
emergency room with severe opisthotonic posturing of her neck and upper
back. She was given 20 mg of intravenous diazepam with resolution of the
muscle spasms after one hour. She reported a 20 year history of chronic
neck and back pain following multiple motor vehicle accidents. However,
her symptoms worsened ten years ago when she began to have episodic
muscle spasms which improved with oral diazepam treatment. Spasms
were precipitated by emotional distress, loud noises, noxious smells, touch,
and movement. Her examination revealed marked hypertrophy of neck,
thoracic paraspinal, and abdominal muscles only involving her right side.
Flexion of her trunk was limited to 60 degrees. She also had abnormal
posturing of her right hand in a clawed position with postural arm exten-
sion only. Writing was normal. The remainder of her neurological exam-
ination was intact. Anti-GAD antibodies was negative.
A review of the literature since 1966 did not reveal any previous case of
asymmetric axial muscle involvement in Stiff-Person syndrome. The only
asymmetric presentations that have been described were those with focal
limb involvement.
Conclusion: This is the ﬁrst case of documented Stiff-Person syndrome
with marked asymmetric axial muscle involvement. The pathophysiology
of this unusual presentation is unclear but may be related to the absence of
anti-GAD antibodies.
P779
Successful treatment of recalcitrant restless legs syndrome with botu-
linum toxin A
K. M. Kudelko, J. S. Rotenberg, M. P. DiFazio, B. Jabbari (Washington,
DC, USA)
Objective: To describe the effective use of repeated doses of Botulinum
Toxin A for the treatment of recalcitrant restless leg syndrome (RLS).
Background: Restless leg syndrome is a common disorder of uncom-
fortable sensations, usually affecting the lower extremities. It is character-
ized by discomfort associated with an irresistible urge to move the legs,
occurring in the evening while attempting to initiate and maintain sleep.
Patients are forced to move to relieve the discomfort. Reduction in effec-
tive sleep time and daytime somnolence results. Additionally, periodic
limb movements (PLMS) may also occur during sleep. Treatment for
restless leg syndrome commonly involves dopaminergic medications.
However, rebound phenomenon is common, and patients often experience
tolerance and augmentation, with symptoms spreading to other regions and
becoming more severe. Alternative medications, including benzodiaz-
epines, opioid analgesics, and clonidine, are also associated with the
potential for tolerance and abuse. Botulinum toxin is an injectable medi-
cation with limited systemic side effects. It has been used for the treatment

of a variety of movement disorders, and has recently been found to be
effective in the treatment of recalcitrant tic and Tourette syndrome. In this
disorder, patients are plagued by a premonitory urge, characterized by an
uncomfortable sensation that precedes tics, which is associated with an
irresistible urge to perform the tic.
Methods: A patient with well-documented RLS, and frequent PLMS
(PLMS index 15.23), unresponsive to oral medication, was offered botu-
linum toxin for his symptoms. This patient had experienced minimal relief
with conventional therapy, with signi ﬁcant side effects, the most problem-
atic of which was an exacerbation of daytime somnolence.
Results: The patient responded well to leg injections of 50 units of
botulinum toxin A divided into 25 unit increments into the Tibialis Ante-
rior muscles bilaterally, with a signi ﬁcant improvement in Epworth sleep-
iness scale. He experienced minimal adverse effects and continued good
response with decreased parasthesias over 3 dosing cycles to date. Daytime
somnolence was signi ﬁcantly improved, and he was able to decrease the
use of oral medications.
Conclusions: Our patient demonstrated a consistent, signi ﬁcant improve-
ment in his symptoms and overall quality of life. This report should prompt
further investigation into the potential use of botulinum toxin for the
treatment of RLS.
P780
Suppression of syncopes after botulinum toxin treatment
E. Moro, P. Cortelli (Milano, Italy; Modena, Italy)
We report a case about the effectiveness of botulinum toxin injections
administered for hyperhidrosis in resolving syncope.
Background: Botulinum toxin type A (BTX-A) is an effective treatment
for dystonia and many other disorders. Armpit, palm and sole hyperhidro-
sis also seem to have a very good response to BTX-A. To our knowledge
there are no reports on the use of BTX-A for neuromediated syncope
secondary to hyperhidrosis.
Methods: A 17-year old man was admitted to Emergency because of one
of the numerous episodes of syncope from which he had suffered for 2
years. For 3 years he had also had severe idiopathic hyperhidrosis in his
armpits and on his back, having to change clothes several times a day. The
many vascular and neurological tests for the syncopes, (echocardiogram,
Holter EKG, EEG, autonomic tests, etc.), identi ﬁed no abnormalities. We
decided to perform a DH and to administer BTX-A for his hyperhidrosis.
A total of 90 UI of Botox were injected subcutaneously in both armpits.
Results: Our DH discovered no abnormalities so we decided to consider
the patient for a “loop recorder ” implant. Some weeks after the BTX
injections were given, we were surprised to learn from the patient that he
had never fainted since treatment. BTX was effective in reducing hyper-
hidrosis by about 90% for both armpits and back although ten months after
the ﬁrst BTX treatment the patient started to sweat again and to experience
presyncopal malaise. We repeated a complete autonomic system evaluation
which conﬁrmed normal control of the cardiovascular system with reduced
tolerance to prolonged orthostatic stress. A new treatment with 100 UI of
Botox was decided on, both for hyperhidrosis and to prevent syncopes.
Conclusions: Our patient suffered from episodes of loss of conscious-
ness which can be classi ﬁed clinically as neuromediated syncope. Auto-
nomic and cardiological evaluation excluded other causes. The complete
resolution of syncopes after the BTX treatment suggested the following

hypothesis: due to his severe hyperhidrosis the patient developed a hypo-
volemic and hyponatriemic condition that, combined with other external
and congenital factors, could be the basis of the cardiovascular instability
leading to a reduced orthostatic tolerance.
P781
Task force on childhood motor disorders consensus report: Classi ﬁ-
cation and de ﬁnition of hypertonic disorders in childhood
T. D. Sanger, M. R. Delgado, L. Dure, D. Gaebler-Spira, M. Hallett,
J. W. Mink (Stanford, CA; Dallas, TX; Birmingham, AL; Chicago, IL;
Bethesda, MD; Rochester, NY, USA)
We report the consensus outcome of an interdisciplinary workshop held
at the National Institutes of Health in April 2001. The purpose of the
workshop was to de ﬁne the terms “spasticity”, “dystonia”, and “rigidity”,
as they are used to describe clinical features of hypertonia in children. The
deﬁnitions were designed to allow differentiation of clinical features even
when more than one feature is simultaneously present, and they represent
clariﬁcations and modi ﬁcations of currently-accepted de ﬁnitions. Subse-
quently, the group met in Dallas in January 2002 to test candidate rating
scales based on the de ﬁnitions.27 clinicians from different ﬁelds each
examined 14 children with varying hypertonic symptoms during a one-day
clinical rating exercise. Clinical ratings tested 60 questions from 4 different
candidate scales.
The results of the clinical rating show that individual clinicians were
consistent with the proposed de ﬁnitions of spasticity, dystonia, and rigidity
